utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, before we start, Mr. Lukic, I just wanted to correct yesterday's ruling on whether or not the other parties can ask questions to Mr. Tadic. I was thinking of the confrontation of one witness against the other, yes, they can. So I do hope that they will indicate to the Prosecution how much time they will take so that the Prosecution can prepare their time for their questions for cross-examination. So let's continue. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Lukic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours good morning all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tadic. Yesterday, when we mentioned Zasavica, you said that one of your brothers-in-law from that village was a Croat, can you give us some more relevant information about your family to show what your relations were with other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first thing I would like to say has to do with the sufferings of my family in World War II.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What the Judge asked you about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes very briefly. In World War II my entire family was victimised, perished. My parents, my grandparents, my uncle and another 15 or so of my relatives all bearing the last name of Tadic. Only four of us remain, four of us children. I was the eldest. I was seven and a half years old. My youngest brother was one and a half years old. We grew up with a grandmother, or rather, it was an old lady who was my grandfather's stepmother. After that I went to an orphanage for war orphans in one place --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the place.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And my brother went to Maribor [phoen] to a home in Maribor, an orphanage which is in Slovenia. My wife was in an orphanage in Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you repeat the place where you were in an orphanage?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Lukavac, this is near Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all we needed. It didn't enter the record, the rest is in the record.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it very briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now please answer Judge Williams' question as to what you know about the way your parents were killed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were killed by the Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to what I asked you, did the past history of your family in any way affect your attitude toward the Croatian population and tell me about the mixed marriages in the Tadic family, we have already heard about your daughter, were there any other mixed marriages in your family with Croats?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that my two nieces were married to Croats, my sister's daughters. My brother is also married to a Croat. My sister is married to a Muslim. About 40 members of the Tadic family are in mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now go back to what we talked about yesterday. We will speak of exchanges, I will remind you of the testimony of Mrs. Jelena Kapetanovic who said that in October she wanted to board a bus, she was told she was to be exchanged and when she arrived, the policeman wouldn't let her on the bus, you remember her testimony to that effect? I ask that the witness be shown Exhibit D67/3. Was it possible, Mr. Tadic, if the list was completed and agreed on, was it possible to add on a name subsequently or to remove a name from the list after the lists had already been agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everything's possible, but it didn't happen. This was not what usually happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My second question: Was it possible for someone to be exchanged whose name was not on the list?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one could board a bus who was not on the list. I remember a neighbour of mine called Nijaz, he was a Muslim who wanted to go and he managed to sneak on to the bus unnoticed and in Crkvina somebody noticed him and one of the members of the escort took him off the bus in Crkvina. This Nijaz was exchanged later when his name was on the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One more question. Why did you have to prevent people who were not on the list from going to the exchange? What sort of problems would arise if someone whose name was not on the list tried to go to the demarcation line, what would happen?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I said there were very many checkpoints and later on perhaps I will explain what the situation was in Gradiska itself, somebody could always check the list, it might occur to them to go and check. This happened very rarely, but someone might think of checking whether the people on the bus were actually the same people on the list and if there were any discrepancies, a very difficult situation might arise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please look at this document? Can you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 7th of October, 1992, this is the exchange that Jelena Kapetanovic wanted to join and you can see that her name is not on this list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this list drawn up ahead of time? Is this a list of people who were to be exchanged on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This list was drawn up by the Red Cross when it had been agreed upon, they would type it out. They had the appropriate service and the typewriter and they were able to type out these lists and the list is final.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now ask that the witness be shown document D68/3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at this list?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the list of the 5th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the first exchange after that one?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's one of the first exchanges that took place afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look at number 31?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she's listed here as Jelena Stanisic. It was easier for her to cross over into Croatia with this last name than with the last name of Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that she needed guarantees to go to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably someone from the Croatian side would have to be looking for her and we heard that she was from that area although at that time, I didn't know where she was from. I didn't know that she had brothers either. I didn't know that her sister lived in Samac who was a ham radio operator. It was only later that I heard that she was claiming I hadn't allowed her to be exchanged. I know that her brothers were in the HVO [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, did you tell her that everybody would be exchanged but that it wouldn't be so easy for her to leave?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no reason to stop her from going or to allow her to go. If someone was looking for her and if she had applied, then she would have to wait her turn. She could have applied a month before, but if there were no exchanges in the intervening period, then she couldn't have gone. It's obvious that she went in November 1992. Before that, she probably didn't want to leave because her boyfriend was there who was 12 years younger than she was and until he swam across the River Sava, it never crossed her mind to go to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know that he swam across the River Sava in August, between that time and November, do you remember how many exchanges were organised?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one, the one she wanted to join but she wasn't on the list then so she wasn't exchanged at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There is something here in the transcript that witness did not say it's on page 5, row 11. Here it says I know that her brothers were in the HVO. This is completely different from what the witness said so maybe my colleague can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, can I have that corrected?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the witness said the opposite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that her brothers were in the HVO and that her sister was a ham radio operator?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I didn't even know she had brothers so how could I have known that her brothers were in the HVO? And it was here in the Court that I heard that her sister was a ham radio operator and that she lived in Samac. I learned some things later on, but at that time, I had no idea about her sister or her being a ham radio operator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now that we are discussing checkpoints, I would like to give Mr. Tadic a blank sheet of paper so that he can make a sketch of the roads around Dragalic where most of the exchanges took place and this is a very important place because of these lists and these checkpoints. So Mr. Tadic, if you could make a sketch please. Your movements at the approach to Dragalic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road from Samac to Dragalic is approximately 250 kilometres long and at first, the route was via Modrica, Rudanka, Stanar, Prnjavor, Klasnica to Gradiska. Later on, the route went through Derventa, Prnjavor, so these were the two routes that were used. The first one, while there were war operations going on around Dvor and Derventa and later on we used the shorter route through Derventa. Gradiska is a border crossing. And from this direction here, from this direction, one would reach Gradiska. This is the River Sava. The first checkpoint was here. This is the police of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you mark it with number one?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number one. When the buses arrived and witnesses have already mentioned this, they would stop here, approximately. Here, there was a small park with a few benches and there was some sort of institution behind it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you mark it with number two?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a small park here with a few benches and there was some sort of institution behind it. Here, there was a coffee shop and this was a shop so when people left the buses, they were able to enter the coffee shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please mark the coffee shop with three and the buses with four?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the cafe that has frequently been mentioned was across the road and it was located here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's number five.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a garden around it and if the weather was nice, then I would go there and people would see me there. When the formalities were completed here and these varied from case to case, that's the River Sava, so the formalities varied from case to case depending on the mood of the people there, on how well I was cooperating with them, and so on, but for the most part, all this happened in a very correct way with a few exceptions. I tried to explain to them that a control had been carried out in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who are they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The policemen manning the checkpoint. I tried to explain to them that everything had been checked, that everything had been done properly and very often, I would take the escort along, a policeman or two from Samac to confirm what I told them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it that was controlled or checked in the case of these people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything starting from the list to the things they were taking with them they could take anything they liked but we would check that they had no weapons, so that was the procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, go on?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you crossed the River Sava on the other side here, on the other bank was the checkpoint of the Nepalese Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mark it with number six please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here there were members of the Nepalese Battalion of the UN and they would check everything too. Mostly they would check the number of people on the bus to see if it tallied with the number of people on the list. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, for the sake of clarity, the witness said we would check they had no weapons, and that was the procedure. I wonder who checked. It might be of benefit to the Chamber, was it the people who loaded them on to the buses in Bosanski Samac or is he referring to checkpoints along the way or both.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was tasked with checking and searching people for weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main check was conducted in Samac; however, it was quite superficial. They didn't go into details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it done by police in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the police in Samac carried out this check but it was very superficial. It wasn't detailed they would simply ask, "Do you have any weapons, you don't." They checked for prohibited items and the same procedure was applied here. As I have told you, the Nepalese Battalion always asked to be -- a passage of vehicle or a bus, they would probe the bags to see whether there were any hard items in there and they would also check the number of people. If there were 50 on the list, they would make sure that there were 50 on the bus, you know they wouldn't go name by name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go following that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that checkpoint, some 300 metres further on, there was a checkpoint of the Krajina police, let's call it that, that was the UNPA zone, the area that was under the UN protection at the time and they had a checkpoint there manned by Serbs from this UNPA zone. They had a checkpoint there and they were quite strict so to speak and they were known to cause trouble frequently but not a lot of trouble. They wanted to count -- do the head count and then compare it with the list and then call out names. For example, they would call somebody sitting on a seat number 10 and that person would call back and then they would go through names around that person and so on. After completing the procedure at that checkpoint and the highway somewhere here, so going from Zagreb to Belgrade. So after we leave this area here, we have some 3 kilometres to get to the highway which was closed at the time and then here, we get to another checkpoint and that checkpoint was manned by the Krajina police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Put number seven next to the first checkpoint of the Krajina police and number eight next to the second one.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we get to the second checkpoint of the Krajina police where the check carried out was not very thorough because they would call them from the previous checkpoint to tell them that there was really nothing to search for and then following that, we get to this place which is the site of the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was a gas pump there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. I hope we will see it again at another exhibit, and that's number nine. The Nepalese Battalion was here, this is where their base was and then behind the Nepalese Battalion was the checkpoint of the Croatian police so they had their own checkpoints further on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mark it with a number 11. So the site of the exchange by the gas station is number 9, Nepalese Battalion's base is number 10 and the checkpoint of the Croatian police is 11.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That checkpoint corresponds to this one, number 8. They had the same role. They were between -- on either side of this neutral zone where the Nepalese Battalion is stationed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's call the sketch the sketch of checkpoints in the vicinity of Dragalic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I will put the date here, the 19th, I think it is the 19th today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just be given a number for this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be treated as Exhibit D160/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a matter of accuracy of the transcript, because here it says I will put the date on the 19th, I think it is the 19th today I'm sorry. It has already been changed I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you going to say?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to add a sentence to say that you can tell it was quite complicated to get to this site and there were a lot of delays, the buses were delayed. That couldn't be avoided as I have told you at the beginning it all depended on the people manning the checkpoint and their mood had quite an impact on us, the people who were arriving there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us mention something that you said yesterday. After you started working with the commission of the 1st Krajina Corps, who was obtaining the permits and who was giving notice of people arriving for exchange?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The notice was given by Mr. Grujicic so our police, police of Republika Srpska, and police of Republika Srpska Krajina were notified by him. All of them had to be notified in order for us to be able to cross over to the other side or rather to enter the UNPA zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We already have exhibits in evidence corroborating this. Now we shall turn to other events in chronological order. All of us know here, it has not been contested that at the end of November, all of the prisoners were transferred from Samac to Batkovic and I will now put several questions to you concerning Batkovic. Under whose jurisdiction was it? Who had established that detention facility in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Batkovic was established by the East Bosnia Corps and the decision on setting it up was signed by General Novica Simic who, at the time, was commander of the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was in charge of exchanging people who were in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was under the exclusive jurisdiction of the military commissions. First of all, that of the East Bosnia Corps and then the 1st Krajina Corps, which probably closely cooperated but the Main Staff also had an important role in it because it consented to all of these exchanges, approved of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether approvals of the military judiciary organs were also needed for the exchanges to be carried out, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned some things from Mr. Grujicic and from Major Savic later on, the one we mentioned yesterday. He was the chairman of the commission but not for a long time there was also Matija Bodiroga there. Bodiroga, he is also mentioned as Bodirogic but we knew him as Matija Bodiroga. He was a lawyer in Bijeljina. And he was a reserve lieutenant in the Yugoslav Peoples' Army. He had a uniform and the insignia of a reserve lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Batkovic several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned that he was the reserve officer of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, you probably made a mistake you meant the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He became a reserve officer in the Yugoslav Peoples' Army and later it was transferred to the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the time that we're interested in, what about at that time, end of 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time he was with the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get to Batkovic, Mr. Tadic, who sent you there and why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Batkovic is in Bijeljina away from Bijeljina in the direction of Vlaka [phoen] where there is a border crossing that we spoke of yesterday so that there are some 160 kilometres from Samac to Batkovic. Travelling from Samac to Banja Luka, there are some 160 kilometres and I've already said that from Samac to Dragalic, there are about 250 kilometres. All of these places seemed even more distant at the time because roads were poor and to go from Banja Luka to Batkovic to take over detainees or prisoners and to complete it in one day was quite a task. Therefore, Samac was used as a midpoint in implementing the task. So the prisoners were taken over from Batkovic, brought to Samac, where they would spend the night and then the following day they would continue to Dragalic. They didn't go to Banja Luka, they went to Dragalic whereas the commission from Banja Luka would go directly to Dragalic which is some 100 kilometres or they would go to the border crossing in Gradiska. And this is where they would wait for the buses and join the column headed towards Dragalic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you use the opportunity when soldiers were exchanged and some of them were from Samac, to take part in it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we get the answer, the interpreters asked whether you could -- asked you to repeat the question, I think they didn't get everything. And also the pause is becoming narrower and narrower between after your question and the answer of Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, meaning the commission from Samac, did you avail yourself of the opportunity when detainees from Batkovic were exchanged, those that were originally from Samac and if there was a possibility for their families to come along if they wanted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that had been pre-agreed, then that's how it happened in addition to those from Batkovic who were usually on a separate bus, I say usually, because it wasn't a rule, it wasn't a rule that we adhered to strictly. However, civilians would join in, those that had been prearranged. If there were only few prisoners from Batkovic, then the bus would be filled up with civilians, the remaining seats would be filled up with civilians. If there were more prisoners then they would be on a separate bus and civilians would be on a separate bus so it just depended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The name of Sabah Seric has been mentioned before this Chamber, the exchange that took place on the 24th of December 1992. I don't want to put a list in front of you but you probably know very well this. Let's clarify this first, is there another person in Samac with a similar name that you are aware of or is there just one single person with that first name and last name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no other person Saban [as interpreted] Seric the son of Hasan was my student, a salesman. His father was an acquaintance of mine we knew each other very well and that is the only Hasan Seric in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the name Saban or Sabah?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sabah.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction Sabah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a correction there is an H on the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said clearly Sabah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this first, was it possible to take somebody from Batkovic to an exchange who was not on the list and for whom approval had not been obtained, was it possible to do that, to take somebody out of Batkovic under these conditions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the approval for the exchange was given by the Main Staff, in that case, nobody would overrule that, nobody even tried to do that. As we will see later, the approval of the Main Staff was requested for all exchanges and this was done by the military commissions, they were the ones who asked for approval as did the judicial organs that were involved in investigations. So the approval was necessary and nobody tried to position themselves above the Main Staff and overrule their decision nor did the first Bosnia or 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mean the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether that man offered you any money, did you ask any money from him or from anyone else in Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I never asked for any money from anybody, nor did I ever take any money from anybody. All of them knew me quite well and they wouldn't dare do that, I'm sure of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there something peculiar on that occasion when they were taken from Batkovic in December of 1992 to the exchange site, what happened in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the exchange described here by one of the witnesses. I don't know whether that was a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was a protected witness, but Their Honours will remember that witness?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. It was quite cold then and I didn't travel in my own car then to Batkovic whereas previously I always did. I travelled on the bus on that occasion, the bus was quite good, so I was on the bus and when we took over the prisoners there, the situation was usually such that I would have a list and the same list was in the hands of the warden of the prison in Batkovic. So I would go to his office and then he would send one of the men working in security there or his deputy to go out and call the names of those people and they would usually line up in front of his office. There was a window there and I could see them through the window lining up in front of the office. When the procedure was over, I would go out and I would say good-bye to them and they would enter the bus or I would greet them and then they would enter the bus and I would enter the bus as well. Since this is quite far, about 100 kilometres, the bus doesn't go all that fast so we spent a lot of time together. There was all kinds of talk and one of the detainees who was closest to me and I was sitting in the front seat said, is it possible for him to get glasses from his home and also some underwear so that he could change, a change of clothes. I said that that would not be a problem that we would manage to do that somehow and then on the road to Samac I thought about how to do this and when we arrived in front of the pensioner's hall, there were about -- it was about 9.00 or 10.00 at night so it was around that time approximately and I suddenly said to all of them, "If anybody has anywhere to spend the night, can they put their hands up." And about 20 of them put their hands up, raised their hands and I told them, "Go, spend the night, have a bath, and tomorrow, come to the school centre from where we will continue on our way." The policeman who was in the escort was surprised and also the people were surprised and perhaps I, myself, was also surprised. He complained a little bit about what the boss would say to me and in order to calm him down, and to take the responsibility off him, I told him, "Tell the boss that this was my decision." I didn't consult him. I wanted him to say that in order to protect the police officer so I asked the policeman and the rest of the people who remained on the bus, there were about 7 or 8 of them, I think, but not too many remained, I asked the staff to take them to the school centre because a classroom was prepared for them. It had been heated so that they could spend the night in that classroom. He was a little angry, I don't know, he didn't feel comfortable but he said, "Very well, I will tell the boss that this is your order." I said, "You just tell the boss," and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He drove them to the school centre?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the next day we were all gathered together when it was time to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Todorovic mind this just like some other things?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His boss was Mr. Todorovic and he wasn't happy about it. He would often tell me as a sort of remark about such acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document D75/3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you said a little while ago about who gave approval and who decided about who could and who could not go from Batkovic, please look at this document and just give me your comment about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can you just repeat the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D75/3 ter.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this document, besides the fact that it speaks in its first part about the way, and here it says, "We were granted abolition" and you know better than I do what that is, we were granted abolition and that's what approximate states in line two and we are immediately passing it on. But what is specific about this document is actually -- I would like to say another thing about it. These two people, Drljacic, Sefo, son of Avdo, and Drljacic, Muharem they are both sons of Avdo Kule. This is what they called him. And the kiosk that we indicated before, you probably remember, they had a grocery store there when I was explaining near my house. They had a grocery store and we were very good acquaintances and as you know they were both in Batkovic and the next person you can see that this was a major exchange because under number 134, there is Kemal Bobic son of Saliha, that's a witness who was here. They were planned to be exchanged on the date that is stated up here on the document; however, the military authorities decided to send some other people instead of them and that is what it states here that they should be taken off the list and that instead of them, these other people should be placed on the list. So I would have been very happy if those people had gone because I didn't know these other people but this is how it happened. So this is why these people remained in prison longer than they were supposed to. This was a decision by the military authorities and we acted in accordance with it so my people that I knew were taken from the list and other people were placed on the list instead of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Witness Grujicic will probably testify about that because he was the one who actually compiled this document. The next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please just for the sake of clarity regarding this document I have a note on my exhibit that the word "abolition" was substituted for the word "pardon" and I have a memory that as I stand here on my feet I haven't checked the transcript obviously, but my memory tells me that that's in fact what happened. It's in the first three lines of the document. I wonder if Defence counsel can shed any light on that concern of mine. I know that the translation, the official translation uses the word "the receipt of abolition" but "pardon" was used. It may or may not be important, I don't know, but that's what my note on the document says and it's also what my memory tells me so I don't know if Defence counsel think it's a matter worth clarifying or if indeed the Chamber does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot now just say it off the top of my head but I think this was discussed during the testimony of Witness Kemal Bobic because that was when this document was introduced. I know the original uses the word "abolition" as read by Mr. Tadic so we will check this so that we don't waste time now and then I will inform the Prosecution about it. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown please document with the internal marking PDB 75/3. I just want to cover quickly an exchange which hasn't been discussed so far, this is the exchange on the 7th of January, 1993 on the orthodox Christmas. Could the witness also then be shown document PDB 76/3 at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document has this date at the top, the 7th of January, 1993 and it's a list of people who were exchanged then. I wanted to comment this bottom part of the list. As you can see, under number 31, is Safet Izetbegovic. Safet Izetbegovic is the brother of Izo Izetbegovic who was a witness here. This is his brother. He's a little bit older than Izo and I knew him just as well as I knew Izo. During the war he was quite sick. He had to go for dialysis and his wife requested, if possible, that he leaves Samac and goes somewhere where he would be more assured of getting dialysis but I said that I wasn't sure that she had to obtain a document from Croatia that somebody was willing to take him in there and then at the first opportunity, he would be able to leave. So she managed to get, and I remember this very well, a paper from Hrovine [phoen] about him crossing over into Croatia and then Mr. Izetbegovic left. He went to Hrovine, he stayed there for a short while and after that he went to Sweden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this other list, another list with the same date is actually a list of the persons who came on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the other list. It ends with number 30, just like the first one, while the other four persons were just added on to that first list. At the top it's also the same date, the 7th of January. This is a list of Serbs. These are Serbs who came at that time. You will see that Dragan Tadic, the son of Pero is written here, the person about whom I said that yesterday, he was requested to come there was a request for him from Modrica, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could these two documents be given exhibit numbers please, if there is no objection. MR. DI FAZIO: No objection, if Your Honours please, but they have to be carefully identified, they are both dated the 7th of January.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document entitled list of persons for exchange on 7th of January 1993 Dragalic will be Exhibit D161/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is this the one bearing the number PDB 75/3?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is correct, PDB 75/3 will be Exhibit D161/3 and ter for the B/C/S. The internal document PDB 76/3 entitled list of persons who came to be exchanged on 7th of January, 1993 in Dragalic will be treated as Exhibit D162/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document D34/3? Correction, D134/3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, what happened, you already mentioned that yesterday, but could you please give us a few details, according to your knowledge, what happened to the detained Serbs in the municipality of Odzak after the corridor was broken through. You said that they were first transferred to Bosanski Brod and Slavonski Brod but tell us, do you know what happened to these people later? Well, could you tell us about that and then I will show you another document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Brod was taken by the 1st Krajina Corps and this happened in early October, the prisoners who were in Bosanski Brod, just as I said, at the high school centre and the Tulek company, these were not only prisoners from Samac, they were also prisoners from the neighbouring areas Doboj, Derventa, Brod, so they were all transferred to the Republic of Croatia to Slavonski Brod. They were in some rowing club, that's where they were placed on the premises of the rowing club near the Sava and they were kept there for a short while and then after that, a number of them were transferred to Orasje and they were in the Donja Mahala, this is a small place near Orasje and some of them were in the school centre in Orasje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to finish what I started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number of those prisoners were transferred to other prisons in the Republic of Croatia. I monitored these people, in a way. I was tracking their movements because I received some information that they were in a certain location. The first information came via a television programme on TV Novi Sad where two prisoners were shown who were detained in Croatia. They were from Eastern Croatia, from that area. They were from an area close to Sid and talking for the television programme, they said that together with them in Kerestinec close to Zagreb, there was a number of Serbs from Novi Grad, some place of that name, they didn't know exactly, and then the two of them mentioned a couple of names, nicknames of those people and after that, I got in touch with them and asked them to give me some detailed information and that is how we got to know. We found out that there were about 10 of these people from Novi Grad in Kerestinec. And this document actually contains a list of those people who are actually on a longer list but the list contains those people that I was taking care of. I realise that the list here is much longer, but the people from Novi Grad are Krsic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the number?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 25, Krsic, Bozidar Krsic, son of Pero. He was actually wounded and lost a leg. Mihaljo Keric, son of Jovan, under number 21; under number 13, Ljubomir Dzuric, son of Bogdan; Oliver Danilovic son of Simo; Zlatko Borejevic, son of Ilija, and not to look for any more, there are about 10 of them here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell me what we are interested in in these proceedings are the following: They had obviously been in the Republic of Croatia. Who negotiated on behalf of the Croatian authorities; do you know their names and who was authorised to release these people from Croatia? Who was the negotiator in view of the fact that these were prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Croatian side, that is the side of the Croatian state, the negotiator was Ivan Grujic and to this day, he is still the president of the commission. Now he is a colonel by rank. Apart from him, he have already mentioned Mr. Marko Milos, who at that time worked with me and still does and I often see them on television as taking part in certain activities and there was another man representing the Republic of Croatia his name is Anto Kujic and he is now retired so he's not active anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was authorised to negotiate on behalf of the authorities of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, it was a military commission, but as I knew these people, I often exerted pressure on Mr. Grujic to tell us where they were, what was happening to them, and this refers only to people from Novi Grad. I didn't do anything about the others because it was the military commission of the 1st Krajina Corps that was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We will now talk about one specific exchange and I ask that the witness be shown document D35/3 and document PDB 85/3.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the documents, it's interesting to mention the fate of one of these people, his name was Lesic, Dragomir Lesic, son of Ilija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes I was about to ask you about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two brothers, Dragutin and Dragomir, one of them died in Kerestinec, in Zagreb. Other people in Zagreb cremated the body. I insisted and kept asking Grujic what had happened to this person. On one occasion in Novska, in Jordan Battalion, he called me to one side and told me what had happened. He said that they didn't have any more burial sites in Zagreb and that they were cremating our prisoners and their own prisoners as well or rather their own people. He explained that to me. I told him that this was not our custom and he wanted to hand the urn over to the commission. I told him well, this was not our custom and I would have to see with his parents and later on, I met his father and his brother Pero who had been exchanged earlier and they said well, let them bring the urn over and that's how the urn arrived and they buried it in the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness said that he had received information that they were cremating Serbian prisoners; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because there was no room at the cemetery?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the exchange of the 29th of January, 1993 and according to this list, under number 29, Witness Nusret Hadzijusufovic was exchanged and he spoke about this but what I want to know is what made this exchange different from others?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While this is on the monitor I would like to say that under number 18, this is what we talked about, Mijo Radic also known as Brada, turned back also Nusret Hadzijusufovic known as Pilja came back and so did some others. This is not so important now but what I want to say is that this exchange was special because neither before nor after this was there ever an exchange similar to this one. We arrived quite late, it was wintertime and we got to Sid at about 4.00 p.m., the exchange took place in Lipovac. We arrived in Sid and an officer came out to meet us. He was an officer of the Russian army because the Russian Battalion was stationed there and he said that only 8 negotiators could accompany him to a checkpoint to negotiate with the Croats. It's interesting to note that there were very many people who had come because they wanted to know whether their people wanted to come over. These were people from Pelagicevo, Orasje, Brkco, and he said only 8 of you, no more. And then 8 of us went with him and 8 people came from the Croatian side. And he said to us, you have ten minutes to reach an agreement. We were in a tent which was about 200 metres away or rather there was a tent about 200 metres away from the place where we were standing and it was the same distance away from the Croatian side and we couldn't say much in ten minutes we just said is everything all right is everything according to the lists. Yes, yes, and that's all that happened. And then he sent a guard to take us back and they said that only 8 detainees could go to that spot without us. So we didn't see what they did there, whether they said anything and I said, "Well, there are a lot of people here so when will this end?" And he said, "No, 8 by 8." So 8 people got out of the us and two soldiers, one in front and one behind took them there and we didn't know what was going on there and then he brought -- they brought 8 people who had crossed over from the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these 8 people tell you that they had declared in front of the Russian Battalion whether they wanted to cross over?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask them but we were in a panic because a certain number of people who had come with me wanted to go back, but we could see that no one was saying anything on the other side so we got into a panic, we didn't know what to do and I said well if you don't want to go over, just say so right here and then go back. So when that short line of fate people arrived they said we don't want to go but the Russians weren't asking anything they said we don't want to go and they left the line. And then we completed the line with one or two other people --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just slow down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the procedure was not logical that the UN soldiers were implementing. And that's how it all ended, a certain number of people stayed behind. They said that in that short line up and stepped out, but had the situation been normal, a lot more people might have crossed over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down, Mr. Tadic, for the interpreters to avoid confusion. Would you please look at the second document, the people listed at the end where it says Bijeljina, Bijeljina, Bijeljina, what is characteristic of these people who arrived from the exchange?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992, there was the 2nd Sember Brigade in which there were quite a few Muslims and in the Orasje area, 11 of them were taken prisoner, I'm not counting them now but these 11 on the list here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Tadic, please listen to my questions. Who took them prisoner?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO, the Croatian Defence Council from Orasje took them prisoner so there were 11 of them from numbers 54 onward. These were members of the army of Republika Srpska, the 2nd Sember Brigade and they were taken prisoner in late 1992 and it will probably transpire later when Mr. Grujicic testifies that he asked for approval from the Main Staff to have these people exchanged or to seek these people and they then crossed over to the Republika Srpska side and 11 Muslims who wanted to cross over to the HVO side left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say Grujicic asked for approval to exchange them you mean he asked for approval for them to come over?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he asked for approval for them to come over, to cross over to our area and return to their units and some of these people have already testified before this Tribunal in favour of some accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I ask that this second document marked PDB 85/3 that it be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D163/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will now talk about the exchange in June. I ask that the witness be shown document D13/3, but before this, I will ask you a general question. Did you, Mr. Tadic, have -- participate in any way in the exchange you mentioned in Nemetin and did the Samac commission play any part in the exchange organised in February by Mr. Krusnare [phoen] or rather the French humanitarian organisations mentioned in these proceedings and did you, as the Samac commission play any part in the exchange of persons who were exchanged in Sarajevo in 1994 and whose testimony we heard here?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an exchange in Nemetin on the 14th of August 1992. It was agreed upon between the governments of the then Yugoslavia and Croatia. The negotiator or rather the person who decided on the Yugoslav side was Milan Panic who was then the prime minister. Then there was a large exchange in which over 1.000 people were exchanged from both sides. This was organised over there and we had no influence or cooperation in that respect, but we were informed by the commission from Belgrade that a number of detainees from our list then arrived. I mentioned Bozic, I think his first name was Rajko who was wounded on the 19th of April, 1992 when Truman was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without details, please just answer my question. I know you would like to talk about it but we have to focus on what is important in these proceedings. So I'm interested in whether you as the Samac commission participated in any way in these three exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already explained about the first exchange, it's important to mention that Milan Djoko Rakic arrived, the one who was taken prisoner on the 9th of May [as interpreted], that's the extent of our involvement in that exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the exchange in February organized by the French humanitarian organisation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no part in that. We learned only later from the army, from the 1st Krajina Corps that Mr. Krusnare took a certain number of detainees from Batkovic and this list included three people from Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Including two protected witnesses whose name we will not mention and the exchanges mentioned by witnesses in Sarajevo in 1994, did you play any part in that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exchange in 1994, we played no part in that either. We had no influence on that exchange. We were simply informed that a certain number of people from Samac were involved in the exchange. There was also another large exchange mentioned here and that was in Sibosnica where one of the protected witnesses in these proceedings was also exchanged about 800 detainees were exchanged on that occasion from both sides in a place called Sibosnica near Ugljevik and one of our witnesses was exchanged there. We played no part in that exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now look at the document. We will talk about an exchange which is important for us and it took place in June 1993 in Dragalic. Tell us whether you remember what happened on that occasion, what happened before the exchange, and during the exchange?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document shows quite clearly what the method was, that this was done by military commissions. I would just like to say something about the last part of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. Tadic. A correction to the transcript, page 30, line 3, you said that Milan Rakic was taken prisoner on the 19th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not in the transcript. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the end it says here we ask the commission of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska up to now I've been mentioning the Main Staff. Now we can see that they had a commission of their own. I haven't come across this before, but it is they who are being addressed and asked to do something. As for the people on this list, you can see that there are witnesses of ours here under number 7 and under number 11, that's what matters. The others are not so important. Number 11 is Mr. Salkic, Ibrahim Salkic who, on that occasion, was exchanged. It just so happened that I went to fetch these people in Batkovic and when I wrote them back, they spent the night in Samac. The following day, the bus left and Mr. Vasovic was probably the one who called out their names, they entered the bus and they started out towards Dragalic. The procedure was as usual, I was driving in my own car and there were no problems with the checkpoints. In the afternoon hours, perhaps 1.00 or 2.00 p.m., we arrived at the checkpoint in Dragalic where the gas station was. Usually, our bus would stop at the first part of the checkpoint whereas the bus coming from Croatia would halt at the other side of the checkpoint, the bus from Croatia bringing Serbs from Croatia. Anto Kujic, with whom I cooperated for many years and with whom I was on good terms, came up to me and asked me whether he could go to the bus to see his prisoners. I said no problem and I escorted him to the bus. There was just the driver on the bus, nobody else and I asked the bus driver to open the door and we entered the bus. He and I greeted them. I did it in my way and he did it in his way and he asked who is Boris Sarcevic who is number two on this list. These first two people here are members of the army of Croatia. This young man sitting behind the driver said, "I am the one." And he tried to pat him on his cheek and the man just jerked away. I noticed that but I didn't know what was going on. I didn't want to be present while they had a conversation. I simply didn't want to bother them so I left the bus and waited for him outside. He remained in the bus -- on the bus for a few minutes and then he came out and said to me, "Brko [Realtime transcript read in error "Brcko"], what's going on with these people?" I said, "I don't know what do you mean?" He said they had complained to him that they had been abused, mistreated the previous night on their way there. I said to him, I don't know anything about that but let me check with the commission and see what we could do about it. When that procedure was completed, and when the people from this list started moving in a column, I walked alongside Salkic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. On page 32, line 19 the witness said, "he said to me Brko, what's going on with these people?" I'm just making a correction to the transcript because it says Brkco in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes and the man addressing me was Anto Kujic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was walking with a group of people, Salkic was included in it and he lifted up his shirt and said, "Look what Stiv had done to me." I asked him whether he wanted to tell my boss about it, whether he would want to repeat it to him and he said he would. And then I called Mr. Grujicic, I believe I called him, and told him to tell it to Mr. Grujicic. And then he said that that night, in Samac, he was beaten by Mr. Todorovic which made Grujicic very angry. He said he would do something about it. And this is how we parted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now pause, please. I would like to ask the technical booth to start the tape for us, Exhibit 103/3 depicting exchange in Dragalic. We will see a brief excerpt from the tape. The Trial Chamber has the transcript of the tape in front of it but we are interested in just one single sentence and the interpreters will translate that for us. Please don't make any comments let us just hear what is said here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Stop here.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This man talking here is Ibrahim Salkic, he mentioned ribs, he said should I show my ribs and he had shown his ribs just a minute prior to this to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What the witness said was not recorded. I don't know if the interpreters were able to follow but the witness said don't tape the plum I have on my eye showing -- pointing to his left eye. [In English] If you just a little bit go back for a --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is fine now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Could you please describe the man?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Ibrahim Salkic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is he wearing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he's wearing a blue T-shirt. I think it's a blue T-shirt and his eyeglasses are hanging on it, I believe sunglasses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To his left is a woman in red and the plum he mentioned meaning the bruise is on his left eye, and it is discernible if one takes a closer look.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Fast forward. We can go faster now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be best to have a break here. Perhaps we could take our break and then show some -- a brief excerpt after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will take our break and continue at 11.00. --- Break taken at 10.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the technical booth continue. During the break I prepared another brief excerpt from the footage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the footage is running, you can make comments, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can hear the voice of Grujicic. These are the Serbs that had come from the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can we stop the tape? Just a little bit back. Stop here. No. Little bit further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell us who is this? Who is holding the child in his arms?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the right, this large man is Mr. Grujicic and to the left is -- you can see me holding a child who was exchanged. This woman had two children and I helped her carry one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of these people whose child you were holding, the people coming out now?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people coming out of the bus, this is the bus that had come from Samac so the people on the bus were Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] A little bit back. Here, thanks, stop here. [Interpretation] Can you comment this now? We see a woman holding papers in her hands.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Biljana Culum, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was her job there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was secretary of the military commission. She had a law degree and she was making records, registering something. These are the Serbs. This is a man from Novi Grad, Ljubo Kuresevic. They are now going from the bus that had brought them there and moving into our bus that had come from Samac. They are mentioning the name of Ljubo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, were journalist teams, were photographers, usually there to report on these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see Salkic once again walking around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] We are finished with the film. [Interpretation] Now tell me please, we saw cameramen there, were journalists and photographers frequently present at exchange sites, was it reported on in the media?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite often especially on the opposite side. There were journalists there present frequently. There was a journalist from Gradiska I can't remember his name but since this was quite close for him he would frequently attend, exchanges, take statements and publish them where needed. I remember one of the exchanges were described yesterday, when we mentioned Branko Mikanovic. I remember him giving an extensive interview in Gradiska when we got to that tavern, he gave an interview to that journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to what we discussed before the video film. Do you remember what measures Grujicic had taken upon learning that Ibrahim Salkic and others had been beaten?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before we get to that, let me tell you something else. Salkic mentioned a man from Bijeljina. However people from Bijeljina never once came to the exchange, nor did they have interest in it. He mentioned a warden from Bijeljina and his task was to get the papers to make records and that was all. It was 350 kilometres away for him so he never attended. He probably thought that it was some of the people present there, because a number of people in the commissions joined the discussion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What discussion do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Discussion concerning the information he provided to me first and then to Grujicic. Grujicic later, on his return to Banja Luka, wrote that report that we had the opportunity to see here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, not yet, we haven't.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, the communication he sent to Mr. Todorovic. This was quite moderate. I don't know his reasons, but he didn't wish to directly mention Mr. Todorovic, but he just wanted to prevent this from happening. I tried to draw the attention of Mr. Todorovic to that, and I tried in a way to say that this would provide a pretext for those on the other side to behave in the same manner. So if some people come from our side, who are beaten, then we could expect that to happen on the other side as well. And after this particular exchange, a man was badly treated in Orasje. His name was Vujadin Cecavac. I suppose that in a certain way, although he wasn't beaten by Salkic or anybody from this group, somebody else took steps quote unquote, so that this would be done to this poor Cecavac. He was even crucified and his hands were pierced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please tell me after this, did you have any problems with Todorovic? We already talked about your problems with the Special Forces and we mentioned some of your conflicts with Todorovic. Did anything else happen specifically after this exchange regarding your relationship with Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My relationship with Mr. Todorovic was always tense. Let me put it that way, and I mostly avoided him. I mean, I never entered into a specific exchange with him of words, and on one occasion, I remember well, after a shelling of Samac, which was quite intense, this was in late 1992, a lot of shells were dropped and there was a lot of damage, and he called me by telephone around 4.00 p.m. and asked me if I had been in town. I said that I wasn't. He asked if I'd seen anything. I said I hadn't. He said that the streets were blocked, there was a lot of damage, and that it would be essential to clear this up as soon as possible. I said that the shelling hadn't stopped yet, there were no indications of that yet, and it was already late, so that everything would be cleaned up tomorrow because we didn't know whether shelling would stop or not. He said this has to be done now and he put the phone down. I didn't act in accordance with that order of his because I wasn't really in charge of that any more but I didn't tell him that. And then sometime in the evening, around 9.00 p.m., four policemen came all young men who I knew well and they said to me, they called me Cika Brko, they said Cika Brko, the chief said we are to bring you in. I laughed and I said, well, all right, I'll go and take a jacket or something. So please wait for me. And they allowed me to do that. I went into the house, I took my jacket and I told my wife I'm going to the SUP and I'll be back soon. I didn't want to tell you any -- I didn't want to tell her anything more. The SUP was in the department store at the time. They brought me to the department store. I entered into an office, and that's where I encountered the already-mentioned Stoko. He was a deputy of the commander or something like that. And another man, his name was Radulovic, he's a former student of mine, and they looked at me and said the chief said that I was to be brought in, and they told me to sit down. I said where is the chief? And they said they don't know. When will he come? They said they don't know that either. So around midnight, there was a noise, you could see Stiv coming, he was drunk, and his hangers on were with him. He barged in and he told the two of those, didn't I tell you where to put him, meaning me, where they were supposed to put me. I suppose he meant the cells, in the SUP, or something like that. And I told him Stivo, what's the matter with you? And so there was a conversation and finally, I told him that he has his own line that he follows and his police and I as the chief of the TO headquarters have my own line [as interpreted]. I have nothing to do with him and he has nothing to do with me. He's responsible to his superiors and I am responsible to mine and if necessary I'll bear responsibility in that sense. And then at the end I told him I have not been the chief of the staff for a year. It wasn't a full year but that's what I told him. I told him I haven't been the head of the staff for a year. And you have nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me Mr. Lukic. Just for clarity, it says here in the English translation, on line 7 of page 39, that Mr. Tadic was chief of the TO headquarters. I don't believe that that's correct. So maybe you could just straighten that out for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said at the time that at the time you were not the chief of the headquarters of the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the staff of the civilian protection. I told him that I hadn't been a chief for a year already although it was actually more six months. And he looked at me in a questioning way and said and who is it? And I said Perica Krstanic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment, please, could you slow down and now that you have said this you mentioned that this was at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was at the end of 1993. I said 1993. Simply without any comment, he turned around and left. Stevan Todorovic turned around and left. So that the three of us stayed there and I looked at them and they said to me, go home. So I went home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because of the name in the transcript, what was the name of the chief of the civil protection headquarters at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the staff was Perica Krstanovic and that is what it states here, Krstanovic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that is why we asked for the correction. Could the witness now please be shown document D102/3? I will repeat for the transcript. The name, Perica, Krstanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what is the number of the document because the number in the transcript, there is a question mark at the end of it. Is it D102/3?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few questions, Mr. Tadic, about your cooperation with the Muslim exchange commission or the commission for the exchange of the federation of the B and H? We had testimony about this from Mr. Maslic. So could you please tell us who did you cooperate with from that commission, you as representatives of the Samac commission? And if you can also tell us something about this specific document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Muslim side, there was a commission of the Tuzla Corps. I don't know which corps was that but its headquarters were in Tuzla, and along with the commission, there were always representatives of the -- of surrounding area, Lukavac, Banovici, Gracanica, Gradacac and so on. These towns that were in that region. We most often cooperated with those places. The President of that commission, of the Muslim part of the commission, was Marko Duspara for a while, a lawyer from Tuzla. I think that he's still doing the same work. Then there was Sefik Mujcinovic, he is now the public prosecutor of the Tuzla canton. Since Gradacac was the closest to us, we made agreements with them most often, and the commissions were in contact with each other through Gradacac because it's closest to the line of separation near Modrica and that's where the meetings were held. Safet Kikic was there, nicknamed Cire. He's a judge, or a prosecutor, at the Gradacac court, and there was also professor Petar Radic. He's probably retired now because he's more or less my age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these exchanges, was the principle of operation the same as the -- with the Croatian commission where people would say whether they wanted to go or not? And could you please tell me why many Muslims and we've heard this during former testimonies, did not want to go to that side but they mostly said that they wanted to go to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the combat operations, the region of Tuzla was in a very difficult situation, economically, because this is not an agricultural area, it's an industrial area and there was a problem with food and there were also other problems, and because of this, and because it was an area which was affected by war, nobody wanted to go from one place where war was going on to another place where war was going on. So it wouldn't really do much for them to go from one such place to another. And that is why the exchange with the Muslim side wasn't very extensive but there were frequent contacts regarding individual cases which were resolved by these commissions and also they dealt with the large number of soldiers who were arrested on one side or the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who negotiated about the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military commission and we were there possibly to try to resolve any of our problems that would crop up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at this document and then comment on it? I think something on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is -- I'm very familiar with it. There are many people here that I know personally. On page 1, there is under number 7 Mustafa Harcinovic. We called him Mujaga. He's a friend of mine. I've known him for many years. His son Esef went to school, elementary school with my son. They went to school together for eight years and I knew him very well. During the war his son happened to be in Srebrenik. That's in the Muslim part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and thinking that he would be able to convince his father to move to Srebrenik he asked to come so that he could talk to him, and I took this friend of mine, Mustafa Harcinovic with me, and then again on page 2, under number 7, it states again that Mustafa Harcinovic stated that he does not want to go to the opposing side. That's what it states. At that time he talked to his son and he told him that he did not wish to cross over to the Srebrenik side, that there was no reason for him to cross over. And so he didn't go to the Muslim part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Besides this time, he went several times to these conversations -- meetings so that he could see his son and talk to him. Esef's mother, Sadeta, also went with me several times to the place where we met so that she could talk to her son. Perhaps it's of interest to mention another case, Safet Kikic has family in Samac. One of his cousins or relatives, Kikic's uncle, had a wife who had to go for dialysis, and Kikic requested that they come over to the Muslim side and I also brought his uncle so that he could talk to him, and when the uncle said that Ferida was going for dialysis, he was told that that was something that they could not provide for him. So he did not end up going and remained in Samac throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who this is?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Avdo Arslanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you we have finished with this document. Could the witness please be shown document PDB 81/3? And while we are getting the document, another question relating to this matter: Was it ever the case that several people were asked several times if they wanted to cross over to the other side?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stating whether they wanted to or did not want to go to the other side was not up to the commission. Insisting for them to be brought to the separation line was on the part of those who asked for them. This was done by their relatives, by their families, and the families would never believe that somebody did not want to go to the other side. It was incomprehensible to them that somebody did not want to go over to the other side. So then after a period of time, on the insistence of the families on one side, we had to oblige and bring the people to the line so that they could say dear brother or dear father I do not wish to go over to the other side, and only then were they satisfied, were these formalities satisfied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at this document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened on the Serb side and on the other side also. The same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please comment briefly on this document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of these lists. It's a list of the people sought after by Gracanica. Gracanica is a place between Gradacac and Doboj in the Muslim part of Bosnia and Herzegovina.
