Under number 10, is Jadranko Suljic, son of Ibrahim, who has already been mentioned here. Born in 1956 in Samac. Now in prison in Batkovici. That's what it says. That's what they knew, rather what their information was. In other places also they put forward their information as to the whereabouts of the person in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If they had information that a person was in Batkovic, who would they turn to to check this information?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part they would turn to the military commission, Grujicic would then ask me or Veljo, whoever happened to be there, whether this person was in Batkovic or not because we knew the people, and we were able to resolve this on the spot. I would say to him, yes, yes, I know that guy is in Batkovic and then we would solve that immediately. We didn't need to go through a whole procedure to check this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume you knew this because these were people from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could talk about certain people from Bosanski Samac if I was certain where they were. But there were others for whom I wasn't certain. And then we would have to check. We would have to go to the house, the address, or call the telephone number that was given. There was a method we used to check the whereabouts of a person whom they assumed was in a certain place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask that this document be given an exhibit number and tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but there is another detail I wish to mention here. Under number 14, it says Ferid Gopo, born in 1963 in Gracanica, missing on the bridge at Karanovac. So it was assumed that this person went missing in that place. What we had to do then was to check whether he was alive or dead, if he was dead whether his body could be found, so these were notes made by the other side to make our job easier. We gave the same kind of information to them in order to facilitate communication between us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D164/3 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We shall now go to the last exchange, December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask that the witness be shown document D96/3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Tadic, what do you know about this exchange?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this information from the end of 1993 boiled down to several basic facts. I was still active in the commission, but I had no office or desk or place to work at. All this was done through the Red Cross and the office of the Red Cross. That's where information was collected, records kept, lists typed out, and from time to time, I would go there and contact them to see what the situation was, what was new and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In December, 1993, where were the offices of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in a building called the social welfare building or something like that, where the social security was as we used to refer to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was no longer the pensioners' club?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. The pensioners' club was vacated by that time. There were no offices there any more, and the secretary of the local commune, a lady who was the secretary, worked up there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Red Cross offices ever situated in the municipal assembly building?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nowhere near that building, nor was there any service that worked with the Red Cross that was located in the Samac municipal building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please comment on the person under number 73? And the following numbers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Cross continued collecting this information, and it is evident from this that people came and reported. They gave detailed information, such as the address, the house number, telephone number and so on, and they would also give information on the person looking for them. So the person looking for someone would be entered as well with details. For example, under number 8, Almir Udzvalic, the person looking for him is so and so, and there is the telephone number. So that you could even -- I knew a lot of these people. This man, Okanovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please comment on page 4? The persons under number 73.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 73 onwards, are members of the Bobic family, Ediba, Bedrudin, Amira, and Faruk, Nermina Bobic. Then there is Faruk, Bedrija Arapovic, and Goran, Selma Arapovic. All of them from Samac. And they were all sought by Zekija Celic at Omladinska Street number 18 in Orasje, telephone number 73249.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Orasje, as the Chamber knows, was under the control of the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in those days, Orasje and Samac had the same area code, which is why the area code is not mentioned here. So these are all the details concerning the search for these persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had the Bobics wanted to leave in the direction of the federation at that time, would there have been any problems for them?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything would have been the same except that it would say here that they were sought by someone else from another area. For example, under number 66, you can see that the person seeking these people was from Karlovac. So there were people all over the place looking for people, and those were the places where they were supposed to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with this December exchange, what do you know about it? I have finished with this document. Were there any negotiations with the other side concerning this exchange and what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the technical work concerning this exchange and the drawing up of this was done by the Red Cross and Veljo. I went to the negotiations, not I alone but the entire commission, and Mr. Grujicic, as before, conducted the negotiations in Dragalic, and this was sometime in early December. Veljo told me that the people from Zasavica who had been there throughout 1992 and 1993 had finally decided to be reunited with their families because a large number of them were on the other side, their children, parts of their families and so on. And they saw that it was not certain that they would be reunited quickly on this side so that's why they decided to go over to the opposite side, and it was mostly Mr. Maslic who contacted them. I never had any conversations with these people from Zasavica concerning their departure. But I knew most of them and I knew about their movements. I met them. I had opportunities to see them at Mr. Dukevic's when they would come to help with certain things he was doing at his house. So it wasn't so strict that they could not go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is testimony in statement number 92, so are you referring to Djordje Dujkovic? And where did he live?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He lived in Kruskovo Polje. This was perhaps three or four kilometres away from Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the war, you saw people from Zasavica helping him? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Even before the war, they had worked together, done certain things together. There is a custom in our parts to slaughter pigs in the autumn, and other animals, in order to prepare food for the winter. Djordje did a lot of things there and I also was invited there as a guest, and there I found these people from Zasavica, some people called Krajnovic and also some women helping there, and I also, in the autumn of 1993, saw some women helping him to pick plums. There were six or seven women from Zasavica helping to pick the plums there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let's now talk about the exchange itself. What happened? Can you tell us when you set out, whether you were part of the escort of these people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't part of the escort, but I went there in my own car, and the bus set out from in front of the pensioners' club, a short routine police control was carried out. This was so to say a mere formality, not the way it used to be at the beginning. This short routine check was completed and then we set out from the pensioners' club, down Edvard Kardelj Street. That's near my house because that was the shortest and the safest route to Zasavica. We didn't have to pass through town and the road was quite straight so we passed by my house and the building number 62, which we have already mentioned, and we came to Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment. Does that route go by the Muslim cemetery?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It goes by the Orthodox cemetery and the Jewish cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't enter the village of Zasavica. The people from Zasavica who wanted to go came out on to the crossroads that we showed yesterday, where the road to Modrica crosses the -- or rather where the Zasavica road branches off, and that's where they were. Of course I knew these people and I talked to them and one of these people approached me and said, "Brko what shall we do? We've got so many things with us and they won't fit on to the bus." Because the people who had set out from Samac had taken up a lot of space. Djordje Dujkovic was there. He had a small truck, and he had come to say goodbye to all his friends. He was there with his truck, and I said to them, well, here is Djordje, let him come along. And then Djordje started making excuses and I said to him, oh, come on Djordje, you will see Juro and the others there. You will see your brother-in-law, because they all knew about the exchange, and all their sons and relatives went to the exchange to meet the people who were supposed to be coming. And in the end, Djordje agreed and they put their things on his truck and he joined the convoy to Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived in Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Gradiska, there were some problems with the police because they had to be persuaded not to take all the stuff out, not to unload it again, but we didn't have any problems about crossing. We were delayed a little while because of the procedure, the lists and so on, so there was a delay of about an hour or an hour and a half. We crossed through all the checkpoints, the Nepalese Battalion checkpoint, the police checkpoint, and then we arrived at the destination which was the petrol pump which was called Sjever meaning north. However, there were no representatives of the Croatian commission there. We waited for quite a long time but they didn't turn up, and then Veljo and Grujicic went to the Nepalese Battalion, which was across the road, and they called some people there, and a representative of the Red Cross from Gradiska arrived, and he asked Grujicic, has all this been agreed on? And Grujicic said yes, it had, and we had come there pursuant to the agreement. Then he asked are there any Muslims here? That's what he said to us who were standing there. And to prevent people saying too much I said well there are a few, just to calm him down, because at that time a war was raging between the Muslims and the Croats throughout central Bosnia, and I don't know whether they had instructions not to receive Muslims or not but at any rate he was satisfied with my reply. When I said that there was just a small number of Muslims, he didn't inspect the list or conduct any further checks. He then said he would try to contact the representatives of the Croatian commission, and that's what happened more or less. Sometime after midnight, it may have been 1.00 a.m., it was December, Marko Milos turned up. He was a representative of the Croatian side of the Republic of Croatia, a representative of the commission of the Republic of Croatia. So it wasn't the representatives of the Orasje part that came, and he apologised to these people. He said, I apologise, there has been a misunderstanding, the people from Orasje, did not inform me on time. And he gave some explanations and he wished the people a Merry Christmas, and then they crossed over to the other side. I think that Djordje had met his --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just an explanation. When you said a representative of the Red Cross of Gradiska arrived and asked whether there were any Muslims there, what Gradiska are you referring to? Was he a representative of the Croatian Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of the Republic of Croatia. Gradiska is in the Republic of Croatia and it's the town closest to Dragalic. It's about two or three kilometres away and that's where it was easiest to reach that man, and that man sometimes turned up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We shall now finish with this exchange but I will ask you: You heard testimony by Hajra Drljacic and Ediba Bobic about the exchange so I will ask you did you personally search anyone's belongings, especially Ediba Bobic? You know what she said before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never even attempted to search anyone, let alone searches. On the contrary, I always tried to protect them from that minimal search done by policemen. I always tried to calm the policemen down and tell them that these people had nothing dangerous on them. They only had their own belongings and this is what I always tried to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, did you ask for any money from Ediba Bobic? Did you take any money from her? And my general question that I have put several times to you during your testimony, is, did you ever, while being involved in exchanges, ask for, accept or take any kind of compensation for the exchange? I mean monetary compensation.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never from Ediba, I never even saw her during the war, and any kind of money is out of the question. Everything she stated is an obvious fabrication. I never had an office in the municipal building where she allegedly came to see me. I never, ever, had an office in the municipal building. If I ever went there, I only went there because I needed to ask for something. The Red Cross was never housed in the municipal building. I never saw her anywhere. So she could not have given money to me in the street, as she stated here. Nobody ever waited for her on the Croatian side in Dragalic to inquire about her Kemo because nobody knew Kemo there. The gentleman on the other side, the witness, did not turn up at that exchange, let alone ask her something. Marko Milos, who was there, knew nothing whatsoever about it. Therefore, all of these were purely her own fabrications. And I'm very pleased that Kemo did not corroborate this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My general question was whether you took any money from anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was fabricated as well. I didn't take, nor did I ask, for any money from anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another topic we need to examine before our final question, very briefly, please. We have heard it mentioned here that you had a beard. What we know nor a fact, what can be gleaned from evidence before this Tribunal, is that at the footage from the exchange which took place on the 4th of September, 1992, you had a beard. What we saw on the videotape today was that in June, in 1993, as well as in a picture from Gradacac taken in May of 1993, you don't have a beard. Can you tell Their Honours when did you grow a beard, why, and when did you shave it off?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had to put these questions to me, but they are silly questions, if I may say so, because everybody has a right to have a beard or not to have one if he so pleases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell us what were your motives? I'm interested in that, and it is clear why the Prosecutor put questions to witnesses here, and you heard what some witnesses had said about you having a beard. Did you have a reason to grow a beard? Why did you do that? Can you tell us that? If you can't, then I won't be putting any further questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any special motives except that we have a custom whereby if somebody in your family is killed, you grow a beard. It is one of the motives. But people don't wear a beard forever. The custom says that you should grow a beard for 40 days, and then shave it off. With me, it lasted a bit longer for practical reasons. There was no electricity, no water, and I frequently went to negotiations, so the beard saved me from having to shave every morning. And on the tape, as we shall see, the Croats who negotiated with me had a beard as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't tell me, when did you start growing a beard? We need this because of the testimony of the witness relating to the 17th of April. Some of the witnesses said here that they saw you around that time with a beard. So please tell us when did you grow a beard?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of my relatives got killed on the 29th of April, 1992. And this is when I stopped shaving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when you started shaving?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I will now turn to the final set of my questions, but before I do that, I will ask you whether you would like to tell us anything else concerning the topics we have examined? If I failed to mention them and you consider them to be crucial for your defence.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm quite tired so that I can't come up with anything special right now. Although I'm sure that there are things that ought to be clarified. But as I've said, I can't think up of anything right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said that I will get to this question. At the very outset, I asked you why you decided to testify before this Chamber, and then you told us about how you surrendered and failed to answer my question directly. So please tell us now. You know that you have no obligation to testify so what were your motives to testify before this Court?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that motive stems out of my testimony. I tried to say before this Chamber what I had to say. I didn't manage to voice everything but I said quite a lot of what I wanted, and based on what I have said, one can create a picture of my role and see what it was that I did during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, according to you, to your records, how many people were exchanged through your commission and the military commission?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we take into account the military segment and the civilian segment, about 1100 people left Samac, whereas about 1100 or 1080 people came to Samac through -- through the lists that we had. So about 1100 people on each side, meaning about 2200 people altogether. This is how many people left and came to Samac area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, when you gave an interview to the OTP, you did not give a solemn declaration. During this testimony, you were under the solemn declaration the entire time and you will continue to be so until you finish your testimony. I will ask you now whether you, through your actions, did anything in order to make the life unbearable for Muslims and Croats in Samac during 1992 and 1993, as the Prosecutor alleges?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary, I did my best to help, and if at all possible, to make life easier to them, not just life but their stay there and everything else. One could say that many of them found shelter in my house, and were assisted by my activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you wish for any of your fellow citizens, your students, the neighbours you knew and those that you didn't know to leave Samac forever?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never even subconsciously wished for that. It was an immediate necessity, and this is how it happened. All of those people returned later on. Their property was restored to them and they chose where they wanted to live, be it Samac or elsewhere. Naturally, circumstances had a lot to do with it. Circumstances that exist now, which I expect will improve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, how did you feel when you escorted these people, who went for an exchange, carrying their personal belongings?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was hard for me, and my attitude reflected that. Somehow I always was a bit distanced from that, so to speak. I tried to be -- I tried to be in it as infrequently as possible because it was a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, how did you feel when these people started returning to Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, most of the people, upon their return, didn't find me in Samac, but during the brief period of time that I spent at home, I met people who had left and returned, perhaps only temporarily, to Samac. My contacts with them were very close and friendly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Tadic: Now, after ten years have passed -- just a minute, please, page 56, line 6, you said that it was an immediate necessity, a temporary necessity. That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. Something has just occurred to me. One of the questions. Many people here spoke about the fact that in some property issues in Samac, about plundering and losing the money they had in accounts in banks in Samac, and it has just occurred to me that we haven't touched upon that subject. So if you wish we can focus on that now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to your accounts in banks?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the citizens who were involved in private businesses had giro accounts, and my giro account suffered the same fate as all the other giro accounts. My money wasn't used and what I had on that account was completely devalued. Just like other citizens, I had quite a lot of money, by our standards. I had foreign currency account with Privredna bank in Samac, in Privredna bank in Odzak, and in another private bank in Tuzla. I also had some money in Dafina bank. To this day, I have not received a single deutschmark back, except for the fact that just recently Republika Srpska has issued guarantees for Dafina bank and promised that in the following 16 years, it would pay out the principal. The Privredna bank in Samac acknowledged the interests accrued. However, not a single penny has been paid to date. The same goes for the other banks I've mentioned. Therefore, the situation is the same for all of the citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, Your Honours. I need to consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, now that ten years have passed from these events in Samac municipalities, and now that you have spent almost four years in detention, do you think that you helped all those people who were exchanged, that you helped them through your activities and your work?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I helped all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've concluded with my examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you -- you're not going to use these other documents so we will return them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. These documents I've already spoken to the Prosecution. Some documents, meaning mainly the list of exchange, I was going to introduce them at the end of my examination, because I wanted to make some checks first because I see that there are some lists which are actually doubled, which were actually tendered by the Prosecution. So I wanted to go through these and then tender them later. So that we don't have to use witnesses for these lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Any other counsel wanting to -- just to put questions to Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Zaric does not want to examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. I have a couple of topics to clarify with Mr. Tadic. Cross-examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, good day, Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I consulted with your lawyer so I have the opportunity to clarify this: Earlier today you spoke about -- this was on page 56, line 6 and 7, when you were talking about the departure of people from Samac. I assume that you meant Serbs, Croats and Muslims who were leaving Samac during the war.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was thinking about the people who left through lists, and there were Serbs, Croats and Muslims on those lists but there were considerably fewer Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That was my understanding as well. Now, your formulation, immediate need -- necessity. Perhaps I'm mistaken but it's better for us to clarify that. I believe that that formulation or that term leaves a certain space for a misunderstanding because this is something that the Prosecution could use to provide a different interpretation. So it is my duty now to ask you to choose between two options that I will give you and to tell us which is more realistic. According to the term, immediate necessity, the departure of non-Serbs in accordance with the departure lists so by immediate necessity, did you mean that they were ethnically persecuted from Samac or the second options -- option that they because of the situation of war, and the joining of their families and other reasons which were beyond the control of regular, ordinary people, were leaving Samac. So which of those two options are you supporting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the other option, the second option, is correct, when I thought -- when I said immediate necessity. I did not want to explain that entire situation. First of all, the area affected was affected by war. Then the economic situation, the constant shelling, separated families, the need for a higher standard in any regard, a higher standard of medical treatment, for example, and so on. So all of these were circumstances which led to the things that I talked about. It did not refer at all to that first part that you talked about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another question, Mr. Tadic: You mentioned a number of people from Samac, Samac citizens, who were on the exchange lists. I think you said that there were about 1100 such persons. So that it could be clarified, because we heard some other evidence in this case relating to that, could you please tell me, since in that context you mentioned that 1.000 or more came to Samac in accordance with those lists, I'm now asking you what was the number of refugees in Samac in late 1992 or in late 1993? Do you have data about this? And can you also explain to us, if that's not in accordance with the number that you mentioned from the exchange lists, how did -- how was accord on that reached, in what other way?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there is this data that you are talking about. The number that came via the lists is much smaller than the number of actual refugees who came to the territory of Samac. We had the opportunity here to see a document, I don't remember the number of it, but it was a report by the Red Cross, where the number 2.800 [as interpreted] Serbs is mentioned, at the end of 1992, and it is stated how many women, how many children, on that list, and so forth. So at the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said on page 60, line 23, he said 5.800 and it says 2.800.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Tadic, it was a correction for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it says 5.800 in the document. Also, it says in the document that at the end of the war in Samac, there were almost 10.000 refugees. So that these numbers are very different. I talked about those people who came via the lists, and these others are people who came as refugees in various other ways. So the number of those who came as refugees is ten times greater than the number of those who came via the lists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my understanding of that also. Could you please tell me, would it be correct if I said that a large number of refugees in Samac significantly disrupted the security environment, the people were angry, they came from areas that were affected by war, from Drvar, Glamoc, Zavidovici, all the other areas. What is your personal knowledge about the atmosphere in Samac, because of the inflow? And if we look at percentages, since Domaljevac and the rest was in the hands of the HVO, so we are talking about 50 per cent of the existing population, 50 per cent more, the number of the population went up by 50 per cent. So what is your understanding or knowledge about this situation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this claim of yours -- MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, there are a lot of issues in that question. I'm not -- Mr. Tadic is not my witness. I'm not standing up to protest on his behalf but there are quite a number of issues in that. If he gives an answer in general terms, you're not going to know what he's answering. If Mr. Pantelic wishes to go into those areas, fine, but surely they should be done individually. Security, anger of the refugees, atmosphere, percentages, they are all separate and on the face of it unrelated topics. Now, the better way would be, I suggest, and for your benefit as well, to divide those topics up and get good, clear answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, well, my first question was related to the atmosphere with regard to the ethnic relations in Samac due to other circumstances, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It was just my foundation but no problem, I can clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What the Prosecution is saying essentially is that break down your questions, put one question at a time so the witness can answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, no problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tadic, to make it brief, because you know how I put the question, could you please tell me your opinion, your personal knowledge, relating to the inflow of Serb refugees in those numbers, to Samac, in the 1992-93 period that is covered by this indictment. Could you please explain that to the Chamber? I don't have to ask you the question.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to answer right away and I said that what you said, your remark, was quite mild, relating to the atmosphere, which resulted from the vast number of refugees. The largest number of refugees were actually oriented towards the town of Samac itself. The large number of people, as you said, angry people, and I would say bitter because of the situation they were in, had a significant effect on life in Samac. The authorities in particular had enormous problems to channel that in a certain way, towards a more or less normal life. This is a vast problem in any way that you look at it, from the aspect of accommodation, satisfying the other social requirements, I don't need to go into all that of what it is that a person needs when they arrive to a new area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, my mike was off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Tadic, and to continue: During questions put by your counsel over the past few days, I think that this was on last Friday or Monday, but you talked about a meeting at the Crisis Staff in April, 1992, when you were called and told that you were appointed commander of the civil protection. On that occasion, you mentioned that Stevan Todorovic and Mirko Jovanovic, according to what you remember, were in a way opposed to this multi-ethnic composition of your headquarters [Realtime transcript read in error "head yours"] and the multi-party composition. Do you remember that you said something to that effect? I'm asking you now, the following: Dr. Blagoje Simic, what was his position on this proposal of yours, the way you found the headquarters of the civilian protection? But just one moment because my colleague, Lazarevic, wishes to correct something in the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: "The ethnic composition of your" here it says "head yours." The thing was Mr. Pantelic was speaking about civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, it will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a problem, yeah in transcript, 63, page line 21, instead of head, it should be headquarters of civilian protection staff, just a correction for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So go ahead, Mr. Tadic. Could you please tell me what Blagoje Simic's stand was towards your proposal to form the civilian protection headquarters in this manner?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember talking about that and that's exactly how it was. I think that even during my first meeting with Mr. Blagoje Simic, told him that the President of the local community would become part of the staff, who at that time was Safet Hadzialagic called Pop, and some other people. He didn't have anything to say to that. He didn't have any objections to that. He said that I should take the people that I believed would be of help. At that meeting, that I discussed, they, and when I said "they" I'm talking about these two men that we are talking about, were not pleased by the fact that the civilian protection staff was formed in this manner, and it's clear that they came out with certain objections. I didn't even notice that the composition of the staff -- I mean I didn't view these people from an ethnic or political aspect, and that they would be close to one another along ethnic or political lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You explained that but could you please tell me, and this is what I'm interested in, the position of Blagoje Simic relating to your proposal. Was he in favour or against?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that he was not against it, and now I wanted to finish. I also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I was waiting for the witness to finish because my concern arises from a previous answer, so perhaps if the witness could finish his answer and then I might raise an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said earlier that these two gentlemen that I mentioned, Stevan Todorovic and Mirko Jovanovic, to any remark or any position, had their own opinion on that and they were quite loud and would try in a certain way to impose what they thought. They reacted in the same way on that occasion, in an impolite manner, because they didn't know what the results would be of these people in their work. Blagoje Simic tried to calm them down, allow the man to do this to the end and then you can come out with your remarks. So in that sense, he tried to calm them down. And he was successful because they accepted that, in a way, but they did not forget to object any time that they had the opportunity to do so, relating to the composition of the civilian protection staff. They would even use the telephone to say whether the staff or the central committee was still in full session. And that's what they do if they wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour it's time for our break of 20 minutes I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, do you just want to raise your matter. MR. DI FAZIO: Just raise the one issue while the matter is fresh in the witness's mind. Mr. Tadic said that even during his first meeting with Dr. Blagoje Simic, he said that Pop was going to become -- Pop was going to become part of his staff, and then he went on to describe another -- an occasion when there was dissatisfaction expressed about that, about his staff, on the part of Todorovic and someone else. In his evidence in chief, the witness described several meetings initially with the Crisis Staff. It's of significance to know whether that particular -- whether this witness, Mr. Tadic, told Dr. Simic of the -- on the first encounter they had, that he had already recruited staff for civilian protection and whether these complaints from Todorovic occurred on that occasion or on a subsequent occasion? Because as I said, he has described several meetings with the administration in the days following the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will take our break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There is a matter of principle. I ask for a break for two minutes more because this is -- it was not quite short submission of the Prosecution. As a matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall take our break and resume our proceedings at 1250 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have one request which I mentioned the day before yesterday. I have received information that my client has been complaining that it's very cold in the room where he is held during the break. Since we are now going to have a long lunch break, I ask, as we are working all day, that the conditions in the one and a half hours during the lunch break be improved for my client, because this is quite exhausting for him. So I ask that the relevant service be informed that the room should be better heated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the break, Mr. Tadic, the Prosecutor broached a topic which he could have kept for his cross-examination, but we can clarify it now. While you were speaking about the moment when you presented the composition of the civilian protection staff to the municipal Crisis Staff, when Todorovic and Jovanovic opposed the composition, were you referring to the day of your first arrival in the premises of the Crisis Staff, and was it on this occasion that Mr. Blagoje Simic supported your proposal, as you said? So just tell us whether this is correct or not and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to the first two encounters and I thought it was clear. The first encounter in Uniglas when I saw Blagoje for the first time, this was not an encounter that happened ad hoc. We met there and we had the chat, and that was the first time when I mentioned Mr. Pop. The second event was the one we have spoken of. So there were two meetings, not more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, my next question, and we have heard a little about this, but as you were a member of the Crisis Staff in the first period, you were not politically active or a member of any party, so was the composition of the Crisis Staff multi-party? Just say yes or no and then we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of your personal knowledge, was the Crisis Staff some sort of coordinating body as you explained that experts from various areas would come there, according to need, or was it some sort of authority issuing orders? How would you describe it on the basis of your personal knowledge and experience of work in that body?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that it was a coordinating body, or to put it in simpler terms, a body receiving requests. It had no function to issue orders of any sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Crisis Staff able to issue any sort of order to the police? Or did the police have other chains of command?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Two things. One is, he's asking was the Crisis Staff able to issue any orders to the police or did the police have chains of command, that's two questions. That's number one. Number two, he's asking him a legal question. He can ask him, did the Crisis Staff while you were on it issue any orders? Were there discussions with the police while you were on it? Legally, that's a statutory issue. So I don't feel he's qualified to respond. He can respond what he knows while he was on it, whether or not orders were issued. And then his answer, he starts, "As far as I know." So if he's going to start speculating or guessing on legal matters that's not for him to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think we are back to the same issue. The witness must tell what happened, what he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour. In fact, all my questions are based on his personal knowledge. So in order not to repeat every time, this construction, for all further questions, as well as for the previous, my basis is according to the witness's personal knowledge. So I think that's clarified the issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tadic, we are speaking of your personal knowledge, while you were a member of that body, did the Crisis Staff issue any orders or instructions to the police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my personal knowledge, and that's what I tried to tell you right away, if we were to identify Stevan Todorovic as a representative of the police, which he often was, I have never heard that any order was issued to Mr. Stevan Todorovic or through him to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour, my colleague just informed me that there was some mis-clarity in the transcript but it's okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question is the following: Did the police have a chain of command of its own, its own system of issuing commands?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly they did. They had their own system of command and just as I, as the commander of the civilian protection staff, had my own line, I was not subordinated to the Crisis Staff but to the Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with Stevan Todorovic, and his alleged role in the work of the Crisis Staff, according to your personal knowledge, did he participate in decision-making or did he define his presence at the meetings of the Crisis Staff in another way? What is your personal knowledge and experience of this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my personal knowledge, while I was in the Crisis Staff, Stevan Todorovic always took a position of power, and tried to impose his own opinion regardless of the opinions of others. And that was the thrust of all his activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have the right to vote in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was rarely a vote held, because the decisions arrived from the expert services, the professional services, and then we would discuss them and say whether we agreed with them, and that would be that. If a vote was held when an important decision had to be reached, Stevan Todorovic usually opposed decisions he didn't like, and he didn't vote in favour of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So the answer is that he had the right to vote?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will repeat the question. Maybe you didn't understand it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No he understood it and he answered. I'm simply asking the witness the position was that Stevan Todorovic, whenever he attended meetings of the Crisis Staff and if there was any vote to be taken, he had the right to vote.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would rather say that he took upon himself the right to vote. It's hard to conclude whether he actually had that right or not, but he took it upon himself to make decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you and the other members of the Crisis Staff and we saw some documents, did you consider him to be a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of his behaviour at the Crisis Staff, I personally was convinced that he was a member. What the others thought, I don't know. This is my opinion, and it was not supported by any documents or -- I don't know -- positions. It's only what I concluded from the way he behaved and the way he imposed his opinions on others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In his testimony, Stevan Todorovic mentioned several times that, after he had committed certain crimes, he reported to the Crisis Staff and told them about these crimes. Did this happen? Do you have any personal knowledge of this?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such knowledge, and this never happened. Had he come and said, "I killed so and so," I probably would not have sat round the same table with him any longer, or had he said, "Last night I entered the detention unit and beat up five or ten people," that would have been so disgusting that I think everyone would have left the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Crisis Staff order the arrest of people in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, the Crisis Staff did not order anyone's arrest. This was exclusively within the competence of Mr. Todorovic and the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tadic, in view of the fact that the Prosecution broached this topic several times, although it's not mentioned in the indictment, but I have to ask you this, I'm referring to the role of the SDS in Samac. Do you have any personal knowledge of the SDS cooperating with the 4th Detachment and the JNA before the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you know about SDS arming members of the Serb population before April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my personal knowledge, the SDS had no need to do that, because all those who responded to the call-up were issued with weapons in a legal manner, with the proper documents, and it would have been wrong for the SDS to get mixed up in this, because this was done in a legal way, it was done in a complete manner, and in a proper way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Am I then right in concluding that the SDS had nothing to do with arming the civilian population of Serb ethnicity? Is that a proper conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, because things were the way I have just described them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question, Mr. Tadic, is: After the 17th of April, 1992, according to your personal knowledge, was the Crisis Staff able to issue orders to the 17th Tactical Group in the area of responsibility of that unit? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, it might be splitting hairs but it's an important splitting of hairs, I submit. The question really should be did the Crisis Staff do that, not whether or not it had the power to, unless Mr. Tadic can be qualified as some sort of legal expert on the emerging laws of the Republika Srpska, and he hasn't been. So I've no objection to asking did this happen but not whether it was capable or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Tadic can answer: Did the Crisis Staff issue any orders to the 17th Tactical Group in the area of responsibility of that unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, there were no such orders issued by the Crisis Staff, either to the 17th Tactical Group which was higher level organ, or to the 4th Detachment, which was in the Samac area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, please tell me, Mr. Tadic, was Crisis Staff able, or did you have any information to the effect that the Crisis Staff was able to issue any orders or instructions to the 2nd Posavina Brigade of the Army of Republika Srpska after the withdrawal of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, the question should be did the Crisis Staff issue any orders to the 2nd Posavina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my information, no, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, did the Crisis Staff participate in appointing officers and command officers of the 2nd Posavina Brigade? In other words did it appoint the people at the command level? Did the Crisis Staff do that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I know, according to the information I have, the Crisis Staff had no such authority, and did not appoint commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me: Did the SDS in Samac maintain, or rather organise political rallies at which it advocated ethnic intolerance? Were there any instances of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend such rallies, nor did I hear from anyone that words of that nature were uttered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you personally know about whether Blagoje Simic demonstrated ethnic intolerance with respect to other ethnic groups in Samac? Did he on any occasion show hatred or intolerance with respect to them in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Blagoje Simic is concerned, I can assure you that he had no such tendencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few questions related to Odzak. The Crisis Staff in Samac, was it able to issue instructions or orders to the military administration in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite logical that it was unable to do that. The military role was subordinated or the military administration was subordinated to the 1st Krajina Corps and the 1st Krajina Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska was subordinated to the main staff and so on. MR. DI FAZIO: Same objection, if Your Honours please. Yes. It's the same -- got the same problem all the time. This witness discussing inherent legal rights or powers, unless he's qualified as an expert in that area, he can't -- he can't talk about that. However, as I've said, I have no objection to the actual issuance of orders or instructions, if Mr. Pantelic asks him did this happen, did it take place, I've got no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's a problem with translation. My question was did the Crisis Staff and it's not in the transcript. So in B/C/S language my question was very clear: Did the Crisis Staff issue any orders so maybe I can proceed on English but it's not my fault. MR. DI FAZIO: No, no. I understand. And it's a difficult matter of linguistics, I understand but I ask that Mr. Pantelic take extra care on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm taking extra care of course. MR. DI FAZIO: And I'm grateful to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will repeat my question: Did the Crisis Staff in Samac, or to be more precise, the War Presidency of Samac, at the time, issue orders to the military administration in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm here speaking as somebody who has certain knowledge. I'm not an expert on that issue. I'm saying this to calm the opposite side. I said that it did not have such authorities, the Crisis Staff, nor could it have done so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know, Mr. Tadic, about the following issue? Did the civilian authorities in Samac, and you know what I'm referring to, to the War Presidency, executive council, the municipal assembly and so on, did they ever, in 1992 and 1993, organise and order the plunder of private property or state-owned property in any way, a systematic plunder of it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was directly involved, there were no such orders, neither did I hear of such orders later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you something about the relations that existed between people that we have become acquainted with in this trial. Please tell me what were the relations like between Simo Zaric and Blagoje Simic? Were they of similar opinions? Did they follow the same kind of policy? Did they cooperate and so on? How would you describe their relationship during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we leave aside their political convictions, which are not important during wartime, at least in my opinion, I believe that they were on good terms. The relations between them were correct. I never heard that they had a clash between them. Neither of them complained to me of the other. But like everybody else, they held different opinions on various matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about their political differences, that is not disputed, but do you know something about the fact that there was a conflict between military authorities and civilian authorities in Samac during 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in it so I couldn't say much about it. According to my personal knowledge, I believe there was no conflict there. We could say that there were some individual, occasional problems but not a conflict per se.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, how would you describe relationship between Blagoje Simic and Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said everything I had about Mr. Stevan Todorovic, everything I believe to be important. I described his attitude towards me. I don't think that he -- his attitude towards Blagoje Simic was any better, and it was even worse towards Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To make it quite clear for the record, did I understand you well that you in fact said that Blagoje Simic was against Stevan Todorovic and held different opinions during this period of time, 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be more likely to say that he was against the views of Mr. Stevan Todorovic, just as I was opposed to his views, as was Simo Zaric. So he wasn't against Todorovic as a person, but against his views.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would you describe the relationship between Blagoje Simic and volunteers from Serbia, the so-called Sareni? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My experience with those people wearing camouflage uniforms was quite bad, and I said yesterday that the same would apply to Mr. Blagoje Simic and Simo Zaric. Their experience with them was quite bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: According to you, did Blagoje Simic issue any orders to volunteers from Serbia? Was he able to do so and how did it look in reality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that Mr. Blagoje Simic issued no orders to volunteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, tell me, please, would it be correct to say that in the time period covered by the indictment, given that evidence was adduced here, certain evidence, would it be correct to say that a large number of citizens of Samac, of non-Serb background, held high offices in various institutions and companies in Samac? Would it be correct to say that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with that claim. And that became clear through the evidence heard here. I've already mentioned some people holding certain offices, such as Dr. Nogic, who was the director of health centre. Other witnesses spoke of other Muslims who held important offices in Bosanski Samac. A large number of these people is living in Samac nowadays as well. Some of them left but a lot of them are still in Samac today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic, in 1992 and 1993, the period covered by the indictment, were the civilian authorities in Samac able to arrest volunteers from Serbia? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I'm a bit confused by the question, if Your Honours please. Is Mr. Pantelic asking whether the civilian authorities had the legal power or authority to arrest volunteers or the Sareni? If so I object, unless Mr. Tadic can be qualified as an expert on the legal structures of the emerging Republika Srpska. On the other hand, if the question is: Did they try to arrest, did they in fact carry out any arrests, no objection at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe also it's the same of -- spirit of language but I will put the question as follows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tadic, please tell us, were civilian authorities in Samac in a situation were they able to arrest -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's precisely what I'm objecting to. If the question could be simply ask did they attempt to or do they arrest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic -- Mr. Pantelic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic is receiving interpretation of the Prosecution's objections. So he should be able to answer, did the civilian authorities issue arrest any of the persons in the -- yeah, in the group of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not within the scope of authorities of civilian authorities to arrest anyone, be them members of wearing camouflage uniforms or not. So according to my knowledge, and I've already told you I was no expert, civilian authorities do not carry out arrests unless we consider police to be civilian authorities. In my fairly long life, I have not seen examples of civilian authorities arresting anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell me, did civilian authorities have any organs of repression under their authority, such as police, or law enforcement authorities, who could have imposed law and order in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this trial so far, it became clear what repressive forces there were, so the Crisis Staff or any other organ had no other repressive forces at their disposal except those which normally exist everywhere, such as police. Since I do not believe the police service to be part of civilian authorities, then my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So civilian authorities in Samac had no repressive forces or police or any other organs under their control, organs that could have carried out arrests?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they had no such forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was any decision of civilian authorities mandatory for police and military organs, any of the decisions passed in 1992 and 1993, according to your information? MR. DI FAZIO: The same objection is made. It's a legal conclusion that is being sought. Now, Mr. Tadic, according to what he has said, was involved in civilian protection and was -- and the commission for exchanges. He was, I know, a member of the Crisis Staff, and again, I have no objection to his saying, giving evidence that in fact they made a decision or in fact he never heard of any such decision, but again and again, the -- again and again he's being asked to draw legal conclusions, namely whether, in theory, any decision of the civilian authorities bound the police or not. So he can be asked did they take any such decisions but not whether or not they were bound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what you know about that, Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already replied that I don't know of any decisions made by the civilian authorities which would be directed towards the police, which would be binding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it time for our break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How much more time, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will -- not more than 10, 15 minutes, even less maybe. I will check the issues here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We will continue our proceedings at 1500 hours. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that I don't have further questions for Mr. Tadic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. The Prosecution? MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, if Your Honours please. Cross-examined by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic by this stage of the proceedings we don't need any introductions, you know who I am and what my task is. However in common with all the lawyers in this courtroom I would ask that if you can possibly answer a question with a yes or a no, please do so. Any ambiguities will be clarified by your counsel later in re-examination. I'd just like to ask you some general and varied questions moving from topic to topic initially. Can you tell me, if the principle of the exchanges was that civilians were exchanged for civilians and soldiers were exchanged for soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me if all the prisoners who were imprisoned in Odzak municipality were exchanged for Croatian soldiers who were in good health and who were in camps or in prisons on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see that there are two questions here. One is who was exchanged and the other is who was in good health and what were the conditions. So perhaps there is a reason to first find out the health condition and then -- MR. DI FAZIO: I'll break it up into portions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, please, Mr. Tadic, if all the prisoners who were imprisoned in Odzak municipality were exchanged for Croatian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly it was like that. The Croat and Muslim soldiers, for those who were detained in prisons in Republika Srpska, were exchanged for those who were in the Republic of Croatia or in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm of course now talking about Bosanski Samac municipality and Odzak municipality. What about that particular geographical area? Would you say that the prisoners who were imprisoned in Odzak municipality were exchanged for Croatian soldiers who were in good health?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In good health is a relative term. Their health was the same on one side and on the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. Were -- I understand that health is a relative term. Thank you. However, can you say that all the Croatian soldiers who were exchanged were in good health?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I wasn't the one who determined their state of health and I can just speculate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know if they were all in good health, the best that you could do would be to speculate?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The occasions that you went to Batkovic, was it only in -- towards the end of 1992 and early 1993, or did you go there on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in late 1992 and early [as interpreted] part of 1993 because the Batkovic camp at that time was formed. It wasn't -- there was no camp there earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the transcript on page 82, line 21, the witness said and part of 1993. He did not say in the early part of 1993. He said and part of 1993. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of 1993 did you go to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that you went there in 1993. Did you go there in early 1993, mid-1993, late 1993? Or did you go there throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that I went there in 1993, partly, in the part when there were exchanges. The exact date of the last time when I went there, I don't know, but let's say that this was in mid-1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also go there in late 1993, do you think?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I did not go there in late 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me if all of the prisoners or the prisoners who were exchanged from Samac to the Croatian side were in good health?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said before that good health is a relative term. I didn't examine anyone or receive any medical finding nor did I see anything in particular relating to health. I saw what I already said, I saw that I had seen that Mr. Salkic had been beaten and I stated that here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you describe the TO, the primary school gym and the high school gym as reception centres where people were put up until they were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The school centre gym is a place that I know very well because I worked at the school centre for a very long time, so I know every particular of that gym. However, I've never been to the gym of the primary school, and I would not be able to describe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is really very simple. Tell me if this is correct: These places, the high school gym, the primary school gym and the TO, can they be described as reception centres, reception centres, where people were put up until they were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could be described as detention until -- where people were, until they were released from that detention. Here we've also heard that people were released even before exchanges took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying, therefore, that those places were not reception centres where people were put up or kept until their exchange occurred?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that. I'm saying that that was detention where people were held up until the point of exchange or up until the point when they were released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say -- sorry, I'll withdraw that. Still referring to these places, the school gyms and TO, would you say that at the beginning of these places starting to function, 500 to 600 people were placed there?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say any number, but if you would like me to comment on what was here, I could say that there were about --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the number of how many people were in the TO.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the school centre there were about 50 and about 300 in the gym but I'm not sure whether these figures were exactly correct, but it is beyond dispute that there were people in those places that you mention. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify something for the transcript, apparently, in your answer you mentioned a number. You mentioned some number. I believe, in the TO, that the interpreters didn't catch. Could you just repeat those numbers again, please?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in the TO, there were about 50 people, so I cannot say 50 or 51, I'm saying approximately 50. In the primary school, there were also about 50 people, and then in the school centre, there were about 300 people. This number was not always the same. From time to time, it was different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you therefore disagree with a figure of between 500 and 600 prisoners in those places? Plus the SUP?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not whether I agree or don't agree. It could be that number but I'm saying I don't have information that it was that number. I can also say that there were about 100 at the TO, 100 in the primary school and about 400 in the high school. So that it would be the number that you are looking for. But it's not anything that I have specific information about. I can only guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So a number of between 500 and 600 doesn't come naturally to you? You wouldn't -- if someone, as I'm asking you now, you wouldn't normally reply between 500 and 600?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would reply that there was not 500 to 600 people at any point. Perhaps I would agree that 500 to 600 people passed through those facilities but I would not agree that at any one point, there were 500 to 600 people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that the reception centres or camps were a consequence of the imprisonment of Serbs in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree, and I don't think that they were a consequence of the imprisonment of Serbs in Odzak because there were -- they were prisons before Odzak and after Odzak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio. Maybe in that last answer, Mr. Tadic, there is a little bit of ambiguity because the translation on line 3 says because there were prisons before Odzak and after Odzak. And necessarily in any state or municipality, there are going to be prisons in time of peace. So the use of the word "prisons" maybe needs a little bit of clarification. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that question -- is that for me or for Mr. Di Fazio?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think I'll leave it to Mr. Di Fazio to rephrase what he asked you to that you can respond without say the ambiguity and as I said the ambiguity might well be in the translation and not in what you yourself said. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you will not involve the use of the word prison. My question to you is this: Would you agree that reception centres or camps were a consequence of the imprisonment of Serbs in the area of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I don't agree, and I said that detention centres, or as you say camps, existed before Odzak as well, and this refers to the 8th of May, about which Mr. Di Fazio wants to talk about. I said that before, there were camps even after the 8th of May, and before the 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But in none of your answers are you referring to traditional prisons that had always existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina throughout the 1970s and 1980s and 1990s -- sorry, 1970s and 1980s?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't talking about classic prisons. I'm talking about the -- what Mr. Di Fazio is asking me about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that satisfy Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. Just the language problem there. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that you were given free rein in organising the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree, because a series of elements were brought out here which limited that. First of all, it was restricted by the other side, which was a part of the negotiating team. Nothing could happen until agreement was reached with the other side. Second, a limiting factor was also the police, which gave its approval as well as the army, which also gave its approval. So I was a technical person in this whole thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would say, then, that you didn't have a free hand in the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV TADIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
